title: Chapter 9 — How to Learn Product: The FAB Framework
intro: The system for turning spec sheets into selling knowledge — feature, advantage, benefit.

sections.title: Why Spec Sheets Don't Sell
sections.content:
I have watched reps memorize entire spec sheets and still lose sales to someone who knows half the specs but connects them to the customer's life. The customer does not care that the dishwasher has a '44 dBA sound rating with a brushless motor.' They care that they can run it during dinner and still hear their family talk.

Product knowledge is not about knowing features. It is about translating features into reasons to buy. The FAB framework is the translation system.

sections.title: Feature, Advantage, Benefit
sections.content:
A Feature is what the product HAS — the spec, the technology, the component. An Advantage is what the feature DOES — how it performs differently than alternatives. A Benefit is what it means for THIS CUSTOMER — connected to their lifestyle, their needs, their discovery answers.

Bad example: 'This Bosch has 42 dBA.' That is a feature with no translation.

Good example: 'This Bosch runs at 42 decibels — that is essentially silent even in an open-concept kitchen. Since you mentioned your kitchen opens to the living room where you watch TV, you will never hear it running.' Feature to advantage to benefit, landed in their actual life.

Every product you sell should have three FAB chains ready to go. The three differentiating features that matter most, each connected to a common customer need.

sections.title: How to Learn a New Product Category
sections.content:
When you encounter a category you do not know well, use this system.

First, learn the configurations. Refrigeration has six configurations. Cooking has ranges versus separates. Laundry has front-load versus top-load. Know what exists before you learn what is good.

Second, learn the key decision points. What are the three or four questions a customer must answer to narrow their selection? For dishwashers: noise level, drying system, third rack, and budget. For refrigerators: configuration, depth, width, and ice.

Third, learn the tiers. Every category has good-better-best tiers. Know what separates a $600 dishwasher from a $1,200 one. Not every feature — the three features that justify the price difference.

Fourth, learn the demo. What do you show? What do you let them touch? The 60-second hands-on demo closes more sales than a 10-minute spec recitation.

sections.title: The Comparison Framework
sections.content:
When comparing products, never dump specs. Use the structure.

Start with what they have in common. 'Both are excellent dishwashers in the premium tier. Both have a third rack, stainless interior, and soil-sensing wash.' This prevents the customer from feeling like they will make a wrong choice.

Highlight differentiators using FAB. For each meaningful difference, connect it to what the customer told you during discovery. The differentiator that matches their number one need gets the most airtime.

Give an honest recommendation. 'Based on what you told me about noise being your top priority, I would lean toward the Bosch because of the zeolite drying system. But if you value the adjustable rack flexibility more, the KitchenAid is the stronger choice there.'

Avoid trashing either product. Both are on your floor. Both deserve respect. Frame as different strengths for different needs, not better versus worse.
